title: NY State Senate · District 31
area: Northern Manhattan: Washington Heights, Inwood, and Marble Hill, extending south through Hamilton Heights, Morningside Heights, the Upper West Side, Hell's Kitchen, and Chelsea.

context.text: Incumbent Robert Jackson defeated Nayma Silver-Matos in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary, 71.9% to 27.7%. He also advanced on the Working Families Party line, which was uncontested. As of this writing, no Republican or other opposition candidate has filed for the general election, leaving Jackson unopposed on the ballot.

candidates.name: Robert Jackson
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary over Nayma Silver-Matos, 71.9%–27.7%; unopposed in the general election.
candidates.currentRole: New York State Senator, District 31 (since January 2019)

summary.text: Robert Jackson is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for re-election to New York State Senate District 31, covering Washington Heights, Inwood, and other northern and west Manhattan neighborhoods. A longtime Washington Heights resident who first became known as a Community School Board president and co-founder of the Campaign for Fiscal Equity school-funding lawsuit, he served on the New York City Council from 2002 to 2013 and was elected to the Senate in 2018. He chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee and is unopposed in the general election.

background.text: Born in Harlem and raised in Manhattan, one of nine children according to his official biography, which says his family has lived in Washington Heights since 1975. Born December 18, 1950, according to Wikipedia.

Attended New York City public schools, including P.S. 186 in Washington Heights and Benjamin Franklin High School in the Bronx, and graduated from the State University of New York at New Paltz (1975, per Wikipedia).
After college, worked for the New York State Department of Labor and the Public Employees Federation, a labor union; was elected to New York City Community School Board 6 in 1986.

As Community School Board president, launched the Campaign for Fiscal Equity lawsuit (Campaign for Fiscal Equity v. State of New York) arguing that the state's school-funding formula shortchanged New York City students, and walked 150 miles to Albany to draw attention to the case. The state's highest court ruled for the plaintiffs in 2003.

Elected to the New York City Council in 2001 and served from 2002 to 2013 representing the 7th District in Manhattan, including as Education Committee chair and co-chair of the Black, Latino and Asian Caucus; he was term-limited in 2013.
Ran unsuccessfully for Manhattan Borough President in the 2013 Democratic primary, finishing third, and lost Democratic primaries for State Senate District 31 in 2014 and 2016.
Elected a Democratic District Leader in 2015, according to his official biography.
Elected to the State Senate in 2018, defeating incumbent Marisol Alcantara in the Democratic primary; re-elected in 2020, 2022, and 2024.
Chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee in the 2025–2026 session and sits on the Education, Health, Higher Education, Housing, Labor, and New York City Education committees.
According to his official biography, he is married and has three daughters.

priorities.text: Workers' rights and job creation, including support for small businesses.
Gun violence reduction and public safety.
Immigrant services and maintaining community services such as senior centers and libraries.

positions.summary: Sponsors S10687, which would require added tenant notices and extra time to respond when landlords apply for major capital improvement rent increases.

record.text: Sponsored S10655, implementing a state collective-bargaining agreement covering more than 56,000 Professional, Scientific and Technical Services Unit employees; passed the Senate 60–0 on June 4, 2026 and signed by the Governor June 12, 2026 (Chapter 133).

Sponsored S10605, extending from 2026 to 2030 the deadline for retirement-system members and workers'-compensation claimants to file World Trade Center rescue, recovery, or cleanup-related disability claims; passed the Senate 61–0 on June 2, 2026 and signed by the Governor September 10, 2026 (Chapter 296).

Sponsored S10590, restoring a 55-years-old/30-years-of-service retirement option and lowering the normal retirement age from 63 to 62 for uniformed court officers and peace officers in the Unified Court System; passed the Senate 61–0 on June 2, 2026 and was delivered to the Governor.
Chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee in the 2025–2026 session and also sits on the Education, Health, Housing, Higher Education, and Labor committees.
